classification.reasoning: Purpose: the crate appears to be a placeholder or minimal shell with only 5 meaningful lines of code and a build script of 4 lines. Sources/Sinks: the build.rs establishes a TCP connection to localhost (TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:80")). While connecting to localhost is often used for port testing or liveness checks rather than external data exfiltration, the presence of a network call in a build script combined with a placeholder-style high version number (99.0.1) and virtually empty library content (5 lines) strongly suggests a placeholder, typo-squatting prep, or dependency confusion artifact. Anomalies: high major version 99.0.1 with zero dependencies and almost no code. Conclusion: While the TCP connection is local and not clearly exfiltrating sensitive data, the combination of an unnecessary build-script network call and placeholder characteristics warrants a suspicious classification and manual review.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: TrapDoor campaign (May 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A cross-ecosystem attack campaign using build.rs as the Rust-specific execution vector (alongside equivalent hooks in other ecosystems). Demonstrated that the build.rs attack surface is actively being operationalized by organized threat actors, not just opportunistic individuals. Attack category: build.rs as a deliberate cross-ecosystem attack vector, part of a broader coordinated campaign.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: proc-macro compiler-level injection
retrieved_context.text: Procedural macros execute inside the Rust compiler at compile time and can inject arbitrary code into the compiled binary, or exfiltrate the source code being compiled (a trade-secret theft vector distinct from runtime data theft). A legitimate proc-macro's implementation should not need std::net, std::process, or an HTTP client crate -- these are the strongest structural red flags for this attack surface, since a macro's job is token-stream transformation, not network I/O.
